explanations.answer: Hunt some game for his father
explanations.explanation: That's the job. Isaac tells Esau, “…go out into the field to hunt some game for me.” (Genesis 27:3) Esau grabs his quiver and bow and heads out. Me, I'd have just picked up a box of cookies and called it dinner.

explanations.answer: Drive a lion away from the flock
explanations.explanation: No lions in this passage, friend. Isaac sends Esau out with his quiver and bow to hunt some game for him. It's a dinner errand, not a monster fight. Thank goodness, because I can barely win a fight with a stubborn jar lid.

explanations.answer: Guard the flocks through the night
explanations.explanation: That's not what Isaac asks. He tells Esau to take his quiver and bow and go out into the field to hunt game for him. No night watch here, just a hunting trip. Esau's heading out during the day as far as the text tells us, and it doesn't say otherwise.

Bless is the word. Isaac wants the tasty dish “…so that I may bless you before I die.” (Genesis 27:4) The whole meal leads up to a blessing. Keep that word in your pocket, because this chapter is going to lean on it hard.

Forgive isn't in Isaac's mouth here. He says he wants to eat the tasty dish so that he may bless Esau before he dies. Nobody in this scene is asking for forgiveness yet. The dish is for a blessing, plain and simple.
No warning is coming, friend. Isaac says he wants to bless Esau before he dies. A warning is a heads up, but this is a blessing. And that blessing is what everybody in this chapter ends up chasing.

She says the opposite, friend. Rebekah tells Jacob, “Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you.” (Genesis 27:8) That's not a stay-out-of-it speech. She pulls him right into the middle of it.

False is right. Rebekah doesn't tell Jacob to stay out of it. She says, “Now, my son, listen to my voice and do exactly as I tell you.” (Genesis 27:8) When somebody says "exactly," you know they've already planned every step.

Two choice young goats, straight from verse 9. Rebekah says she'll make them into a tasty dish for Isaac, the kind he loves. She's got the menu, the plan and the cooking all lined up. I just wish my plans came together that fast.
Not lambs this time. Rebekah sends Jacob to the flock for two choice young goats. She says she'll make them into the kind of dish Isaac loves. Seven is a big number for one dinner anyway.

That ram belongs to a different story. It's the one Abraham, Isaac's father, finds caught in a thicket by its horns (Genesis 22:13). Here, Rebekah sends Jacob to the flock for two choice young goats. Two goats, one dish, and no thicket in sight.

explanations.answer: Esau is hairy and Jacob is smooth
explanations.explanation: That's his worry. Jacob says, “…my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.” (Genesis 27:11) Isaac can't see, but he can feel. Jacob's plan has a very hands-on problem.

explanations.answer: Goat won't taste like wild game
explanations.explanation: Jacob never brings up the taste. What he says is, “…my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.” (Genesis 27:11) His worry is what Isaac will feel, not what he'll taste. Rebekah's already handling the cooking, and the text says it's the kind of dish Isaac loves.

explanations.answer: Esau will be home any minute
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't mention Esau coming home. Esau has just gone out to hunt, and Jacob's concern is something else. He says, “…my brother Esau is a hairy man, but I am smooth-skinned.” (Genesis 27:11) It's about touch, friend.

Curse is the word. Jacob says, “…I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing.” (Genesis 27:12) He's picturing the exact opposite of what he's after. That's a big swing, from blessing all the way to curse.
Jacob doesn't say anything about a beating. He says he'd bring upon himself a curse rather than a blessing. The worry is about the blessing going the wrong way. It isn't about getting roughed up.

A rebuke would sting, but that's not the word. Jacob says, “…I would bring upon myself a curse rather than a blessing.” (Genesis 27:12) A curse is a much heavier thing than a scolding. He knows exactly what's on the line.

True. Rebekah takes “…the finest clothes in the house that belonged to her older son Esau” and puts them on Jacob. (Genesis 27:15) She's not just cooking, she's dressing him for the part. This woman thought of everything.

She does dress him in them, friend. The text says Rebekah took the finest clothes in the house that belonged to Esau, her older son, and put them on Jacob. She's covering more than the menu. Jacob's walking out in his brother's best.

Skins of the young goats, on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. (Genesis 27:16) Rebekah answers Jacob's hairy-versus-smooth problem with the goats themselves. Whatever you think of this plan, she was committed.
No wool here. The text says Rebekah put the skins of the young goats on his hands and on the smooth part of his neck. The goats are doing double duty, dinner and disguise.

Camel's hair would have been next-level commitment, but it isn't in the story. Rebekah uses the skins of the young goats on Jacob's hands and on the smooth part of his neck. One goat project at a time, friend.

That's what he says. Jacob tells his father, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me.” (Genesis 27:19) He's not just claiming the name, he's claiming the whole spot in the family. That's a big one to say to a father who can't see you.

explanations.answer: I am Jacob your younger son
explanations.explanation: That would be the truth, but it's not what Jacob says. He says, “I am Esau, your firstborn.” (Genesis 27:19) Isaac asked which son he was, and Jacob gives his brother's name. Honest answer, wrong brother.

explanations.answer: I am a servant sent by Esau
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't pretend to be a servant. He says, “I am Esau, your firstborn.” (Genesis 27:19) He goes all in on being Esau. No middleman, no side door.

explanations.answer: The LORD your God brought it to me
explanations.explanation: That's the answer Jacob gives. He says, “Because the LORD your God brought it to me.” (Genesis 27:20) That's Jacob's claim, and nothing in the text backs it up. I'll just say it stands out.

explanations.answer: An angel of the LORD led me to it
explanations.explanation: There's no angel in Jacob's answer. He says, “Because the LORD your God brought it to me.” (Genesis 27:20) Isaac asked how he found it so quickly, and that's what he gets.

explanations.answer: My servants drove it right to me
explanations.explanation: Servants don't come up here. Jacob answers, “Because the LORD your God brought it to me.” (Genesis 27:20) The text has nothing about helpers driving anything. It's just Jacob's one line in answer to his father's question.

Jacob it is. Isaac says, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” (Genesis 27:22) The old man's ears say one thing and his fingers say another. Rebekah's goat skins are doing the talking.

Abraham, Isaac's father, isn't in this scene. Isaac says, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” (Genesis 27:22) He's talking about the son standing in front of him. His ears are catching on to something.

Laban, Rebekah's brother (Genesis 24:29), isn't in this scene. Isaac says, “The voice is the voice of Jacob, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” (Genesis 27:22) The son in front of him gets named, not the uncle. Good thing nobody mixed up the family tree here.
He doesn't come clean, friend. Isaac asks, “Are you really my son Esau?” and Jacob replies, “I am.” (Genesis 27:24) That's a second chance to tell the truth, and he keeps going with the plan.
False is right. Isaac asks, “Are you really my son Esau?” and Jacob answers, “I am.” (Genesis 27:24) He had one more chance to speak up. He says the same thing again.

True. After he eats and drinks, Isaac says, “Please come near and kiss me, my son.” (Genesis 27:26) The next move in the scene is a kiss. It's up close and personal, right when Jacob's disguise needs to hold.

He does ask. The text says that after the meal, Isaac tells his son, “Please come near and kiss me, my son.” (Genesis 27:26) Jacob has to step right up close. That's the moment Isaac gets a good whiff of the disguise.

explanations.answer: A field the LORD has blessed
explanations.explanation: A field the LORD has blessed. Isaac says, “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.” (Genesis 27:27) That's high praise for somebody wearing Esau's clothes. I've been compared to plenty of things, but never a blessed field.
No cedars here. Isaac says, “Ah, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed.” (Genesis 27:27) The comparison is a field, not a forest. It's a farm smell, friend.

Myrrh isn't in this verse. Isaac says the smell of his son is like the smell of a field that the LORD has blessed. (Genesis 27:27) He's picturing open land, not perfume. That's his comparison, and it's a good one.

Master, right from the blessing. Isaac says, “May you be the master of your brothers, and may the sons of your mother bow down to you.” (Genesis 27:29) That's a big word to say over a son. And he thinks he's saying it to Esau.
Keeper isn't the word Isaac uses. He says, “May you be the master of your brothers…” (Genesis 27:29) Master is stronger than keeper. It means his brothers answer to him.

Shepherd would be a gentle word, but it's not here. Isaac says, “May you be the master of your brothers…” (Genesis 27:29) That's master, with the sons of his mother bowing down to him. It's a big blessing.

It's the other way around, friend. The blessing says, “May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed.” (Genesis 27:29) Cursing Jacob doesn't get anyone a blessing. This blessing has some real weight behind it.

False is right. Isaac says, “May those who curse you be cursed, and those who bless you be blessed.” (Genesis 27:29) The curses go to the people who curse, and the blessings go to the people who bless. Simple as that.
He's got something for his dad. The text says Esau “too made some tasty food, brought it to his father…” (Genesis 27:31) He did the job he was sent to do. Too bad he's a little late.
False is right. Esau makes some tasty food and brings it to his father. (Genesis 27:31) He did exactly what Isaac asked him to do. He's just a little behind schedule.
He does. The text says, “Isaac began to tremble violently.” (Genesis 27:33) Then he asks who it was that hunted the game and brought it to him. This is a heavy moment, and Isaac feels all of it.
No laughing here, friend. The text says Isaac began to tremble violently. (Genesis 27:33) This is a heavy moment, so I'll leave it at that.
No clothes get torn here. The text says Isaac began to tremble violently. (Genesis 27:33) Then he asks who it was that brought him the game. It's a heavy moment, and the text tells it plainly.
True. Isaac says he ate it all and blessed him, “…indeed, he will be blessed!” (Genesis 27:33) He doesn't take it back. The blessing stands.
He actually says it, friend. Isaac says, “…indeed, he will be blessed!” (Genesis 27:33) The blessing he already gave stays in place. He doesn't take it back.

explanations.answer: Your brother came deceitfully and took it
explanations.explanation: That's it. Isaac tells Esau, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.” (Genesis 27:35) He names Esau's own brother. That's a hard thing for Esau to hear.

explanations.answer: A stranger tricked me at the door
explanations.explanation: Isaac doesn't say stranger. He says, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.” (Genesis 27:35) It was Esau's own brother. That makes it sting more.

explanations.answer: Your servant brought me the dish first
explanations.explanation: There's no servant in this part. Isaac says, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.” (Genesis 27:35) The one who brought the dish was Esau's own brother. Isaac names him plainly.
Birthright. Esau says, “He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing.” (Genesis 27:36) That's the two he's counting. Esau says it's twice now.
Herds aren't what Esau is counting. He says, “He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing.” (Genesis 27:36) His list is the birthright and the blessing. Those are the two he names.
Wells aren't on Esau's list here. He says, “He took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing.” (Genesis 27:36) Birthright and blessing, that's his count. And he says Jacob did both.

explanations.answer: Do you have only one blessing
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks. Esau says, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, O my father!” (Genesis 27:38) He's still hoping there's something left for him. This is a hard part of the story.
Esau doesn't ask where Jacob went. He asks, “Do you have only one blessing, my father?” (Genesis 27:38) He's pleading with his father for something of his own. It's a tender, heavy moment.
Esau doesn't ask for a curse. He says, “Do you have only one blessing, my father? Bless me too, O my father!” (Genesis 27:38) What he wants is a blessing for himself. It's a hard moment to read.

explanations.answer: Away from the richness of the land
explanations.explanation: That's what Isaac says. “Behold, your dwelling place shall be away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above.” (Genesis 27:39) It's the opposite of what he said over Jacob. That's a heavy word for Esau.

explanations.answer: In the well-watered plain of the Jordan
explanations.explanation: That's not what Isaac says. He tells Esau his dwelling place will be away from the richness of the land, away from the dew of heaven above. (Genesis 27:39) The picture is dry, not well-watered. It's a hard thing to hear.

explanations.answer: In a land flowing with milk and honey
explanations.explanation: Isaac says the opposite. He tells Esau, “…your dwelling place shall be away from the richness of the land…” (Genesis 27:39) No milk and honey here. It's a heavy word.
Sword. Isaac says, “You shall live by the sword and serve your brother.” (Genesis 27:40) It's a hard life he's describing. And it ends with serving his brother.
Plow isn't the word. Isaac says, “You shall live by the sword and serve your brother.” (Genesis 27:40) A sword is a harder picture than a plow. This is a heavy thing for Esau to hear.
Flock isn't what Isaac says. He tells Esau, “You shall live by the sword and serve your brother.” (Genesis 27:40) It's sword, not flock. That's a heavy word for Esau.
There's a way out in the text, friend. Isaac says, “But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck.” (Genesis 27:40) So it isn't forever with no way out. The last word isn't a closed door.
False is right. Isaac says, “But when you rebel, you will tear his yoke from your neck.” (Genesis 27:40) So the serving doesn't go on forever. The text leaves a way out for Esau.
